title: Ezekiel 35:1–15
context: The LORD’s word comes to Ezekiel, telling him to set his face against Mount Seir, the hill country associated with Edom, the people traced to Esau (compare Genesis 25:30). The Lord GOD charges Edom with “perpetual hostility” toward Israel and with handing Israelites over to the sword in their time of calamity (35:5), with claiming the land of “these two nations,” Israel and Judah, as its own although the LORD was there (35:10), and with rejoicing over Israel’s desolation (35:12–15). Judgment will fit the offense: as Edom rejoiced over Israel’s ruin, so Mount Seir will be made desolate. Other passages voice similar charges against Edom, including Ezekiel 25:12–14, Obadiah 10–14, Psalm 137:7, Lamentations 4:21–22, and Malachi 1:3–4; they are named here without harmonizing. Historians reconstruct the exact events behind these charges in different ways. The oracle prepares for chapter 36, where the mountains Edom coveted are addressed with promise.

verses.text: Moreover the LORD’s word came to me, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD’s word comes to Ezekiel again. Arminian readers note that the oracle against Edom stands between the promise of a shepherd in chapter 34 and the restoration of the mountains in chapter 36.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the formula grounding the oracle in divine authority. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as introducing a word against Israel’s neighbor that prepares for the promises to Israel that follow.

verses.text: “Son of man, set your face against Mount Seir, and prophesy against it,
verses.arminianNotes: Ezekiel is to set his face against Mount Seir and prophesy against it. Arminian readers see Edom addressed by its mountain, which stands in contrast with the mountains of Israel in the next chapter.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the setting of the face as a gesture of prophetic judgment, used throughout Ezekiel. Both traditions read Mount Seir as the hill country associated with Edom, named here as the object of the LORD’s word.

verses.text: and tell it, ‘The Lord GOD says: “Behold, I am against you, Mount Seir, and I will stretch out my hand against you. I will make you a desolation and an astonishment.
verses.arminianNotes: The Lord GOD says he is against Mount Seir and will stretch out his hand to make it a desolation. Arminian readers see God’s opposition as a response to Edom’s conduct, which the following verses describe.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the LORD’s sovereignty over nations beyond Israel, all accountable to him. Shared ground: both traditions read the outstretched hand as an image of God’s power in judgment, as in 6:14.

verses.text: I will lay your cities waste, and you will be desolate. Then you will know that I am the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD will lay Edom’s cities waste, and they will know that he is the LORD. Arminian readers note that the recognition formula applies to Edom too, as judgment makes God known beyond Israel.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the knowledge of the LORD as the goal of his dealings with all nations. Both traditions read the refrain as central to Ezekiel, now extended to a neighboring people.

verses.text: “ ‘ “Because you have had a perpetual hostility, and have given over the children of Israel to the power of the sword in the time of their calamity, in the time of the iniquity of the end,
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD charges Edom with perpetual hostility and with handing Israel to the sword in their calamity. Arminian readers see Edom’s guilt in exploiting a brother’s disaster, compare Obadiah 10–14 by reference.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the phrase the iniquity of the end, linking Edom’s act to the time of Jerusalem’s fall. Shared ground: both traditions read the charge as betrayal at a neighbor’s lowest moment, while holding the exact events loosely.

verses.text: therefore, as I live,” says the Lord GOD, “I will prepare you for blood, and blood will pursue you. Since you have not hated blood, therefore blood will pursue you.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD swears that blood will pursue Edom, since it did not hate blood. Arminian readers see judgment matching the violence Edom chose, reaping what it sowed.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the oath as I live underscoring the certainty of the sentence. Both traditions read the verse as fitting retribution for bloodshed, and they handle its language soberly.

verses.text: Thus I will make Mount Seir an astonishment and a desolation. I will cut off from it him who passes through and him who returns.
verses.arminianNotes: Mount Seir will become an astonishment and desolation, with no one passing through or returning. Arminian readers see the end of trade and travel, as a land once busy becomes empty.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verse as reversing Edom’s ambition to possess Israel’s land. Shared ground: both traditions read the desolation as the consequence of Edom’s hostility, described with restraint.

verses.text: I will fill its mountains with its slain. The slain with the sword will fall in your hills and in your valleys and in all your watercourses.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD will fill Edom’s mountains, hills, valleys, and watercourses with the slain. Arminian readers note the echo of chapter 6, where the same landscape terms described Israel’s judgment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same judgment Edom welcomed for Israel now falling on Edom. Both traditions read the parallel with 6:3 as deliberate, and they treat the description briefly and soberly.

verses.text: I will make you a perpetual desolation, and your cities will not be inhabited. Then you will know that I am the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: Edom will be a perpetual desolation, its cities uninhabited, and they will know the LORD. Arminian readers note that perpetual hostility is answered by perpetual desolation, measure for measure.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the word perpetual as stressing the finality of the sentence on Edom as a hostile power. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as fitting judgment on Edom’s long enmity, spoken to the situation of Ezekiel’s day.

verses.text: “ ‘ “Because you have said, ‘These two nations and these two countries will be mine, and we will possess it,’ although the LORD was there,
verses.arminianNotes: Edom said that the two nations and their lands would be theirs, although the LORD was there. Arminian readers see Edom’s error in assuming that Israel’s defeat meant God had abandoned his land.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the phrase although the LORD was there as the heart of the charge: Edom coveted what belonged to God. Both traditions read the two nations as Israel and Judah, and they see the LORD’s claim on the land as decisive.

verses.text: therefore, as I live,” says the Lord GOD, “I will do according to your anger, and according to your envy which you have shown out of your hatred against them; and I will make myself known among them when I judge you.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD swears to deal with Edom according to its anger and envy, making himself known when he judges. Arminian readers see the measure of judgment set by Edom’s own attitudes.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God revealing himself through just judgment, so that his character is made known. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing that hatred and envy toward God’s people are not hidden from him.

verses.text: You will know that I, the LORD, have heard all your insults which you have spoken against the mountains of Israel, saying, ‘They have been laid desolate. They have been given to us to devour.’
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD has heard Edom’s insults against the mountains of Israel: desolate and given to us to devour. Arminian readers see God’s attentiveness to words spoken against his people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verse as showing that mockery of Israel is mockery of the LORD who owns the land. Both traditions read the quoted taunt as revealing Edom’s greed, and they compare Psalm 137:7 by reference.

verses.text: You have magnified yourselves against me with your mouth, and have multiplied your words against me. I have heard it.”
verses.arminianNotes: Edom magnified itself against the LORD with its mouth, and he has heard it. Arminian readers see pride expressed in speech, which God treats as a real offense against himself.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verse as identifying the root of Edom’s sin: arrogance against God. Shared ground: both traditions read the line as a reminder that words matter before God, who hears what is said.

verses.text: The Lord GOD says: “When the whole earth rejoices, I will make you desolate.
verses.arminianNotes: The Lord GOD says that when the whole earth rejoices, he will make Edom desolate. Arminian readers take the whole earth’s rejoicing as a contrast with Edom’s fate, perhaps at a time of wider renewal.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hold the phrase loosely, some seeing a time of wider restoration. Both traditions read the verse as setting Edom’s desolation against a broader joy, without fixing a single interpretation.

verses.text: As you rejoiced over the inheritance of the house of Israel because it was desolate, so I will do to you. You will be desolate, Mount Seir, and all Edom, even all of it. Then they will know that I am the LORD.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: As Edom rejoiced over Israel’s desolation, so it will be desolate, all of it, and they will know the LORD. Arminian readers see gloating answered by the same measure it showed.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the principle of measure-for-measure justice, compare Obadiah 15 by reference. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a warning against rejoicing in another’s ruin, a theme found across Scripture.
